content.text:
Operator
Greetings, and welcome to The Chefs' Warehouse Q4 2024 Earnings Conference Call. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your host, Alexandros Aldous, General Counsel, Corporate Secretary, and Chief Government Relations Officer. Please go ahead, sir.
Alexandros Aldous
General Counsel, Corporate Secretary, and Chief Government Relations Officer, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone. With me on today's call are Chris Pappas, Founder, Chairman, and CEO, and Jim Leddy, our CFO. By now, you should have access to our Q4 2024 earnings press release. It can also be found at www.chefswarehouse.com under the Investor Relations section. Throughout this conference call, we will be presenting non-GAAP financial measures, including, among others, historical and estimated EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, adjusted net income, adjusted earnings per share, adjusted operating expenses, net debt leverage, and free cash flow. These measures are not calculated in accordance with GAAP and may be calculated differently in similarly titled non-GAAP financial measures used by other companies. Quantitative reconciliations of our non-GAAP financial measures to their most directly comparable GAAP financial measures appear in today's press release and Q4 2024 earnings presentation.
Before we begin our formal remarks, I need to remind everyone that part of our discussion today will include forward-looking statements, including statements regarding our estimated financial performance. Such forward-looking statements are not guarantees of future performance, and therefore you should not put undue reliance on them. These statements are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from what we expect. Some of these risks are mentioned in today's release. Others are disclosed in our annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, which are available on the SEC website. Today, we are going to provide a business update and go over our Q4 results in detail.
For a portion of our discussion this morning, we will refer to a few slides posted on The Chefs' Warehouse website under the Investor Relations section titled, Q4 2024 Earnings Presentation. Please note that these slides are disclosed at this time for illustration purposes only. We will open up the call for questions. With that, I will turn the call over to Chris Pappas. Chris?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Alex. Thank you all for joining our Q4 2024 earnings call. Business activity and demand remained consistently strong through Q4 amidst a healthy environment for our core upscale casual to higher-end dining customer base. Our teams across domestic and international markets provided excellent product and service amidst a busy holiday season, and delivered the first $1 billion+ revenue quarter in Chefs' Warehouse history and strong growth in gross profit dollars in March. During the quarter, we've continued growing market share, closing the year with strong year-over-year growth in unique item placements and new customer acquisition. I'd like to thank the entire Chefs' Warehouse team for their dedication and commitment in delivering a strong 2024 for our team members, our customers, and supply partners, and our shareholders. Now, please refer to slide three of the presentation.
A few highlights from Q4 include 8.7% growth in net sales. Specialty sales were up 11.5% over the prior year, which was driven by unique customer growth of approximately 4.5%, placement growth of 12.3%, and specialty case growth of 6.1%. Pounds in center of the plate were approximately 3.6% higher than the prior year Q4. Gross profit margins increased approximately 23 basis points. Gross margin in the specialty category increased approximately 22 basis points as compared to Q4 of 2023, while gross margin in the center of the plate category decreased approximately 7 basis points year over year. Jim will provide more detail on gross profit margins in a few moments. Now please refer to slide four.
Chart 1 provides a full-year 2024 update to gross profit dollars per route as compared to 2019. Chart 2 provides full-year 2024 adjusted operating expense as a percentage of gross profit dollar improvement by 24 basis points versus 2023 and 92 basis points versus 2019. Full-year 2024 adjusted EBITDA per employee increased 13% versus 2023 and 18% versus 2019. Now please refer to slide five. The charts here display the progression of customer orders coming via our digital platform, which include orders coming via mobile and website. Investments in our digital platform continue to contribute to margin enhancement as our team drives both online order adoption growth, enhancements to customer-facing functionality, and improved real-time data analytics supporting our sales teams.
As of Q4 2024, approximately 56% of customers ordering through our domestic specialty locations are online versus 48% in 2023 and 20% at year-end 2019. Now please refer to slide six. Slide six displays the five key areas that our teams are focused on in order to deliver our expectation of continued above industry average top line gross profit dollar and Adjusted EBITDA growth, as well as targeted incremental Adjusted EBITDA margin improvement over the next four years. We look forward to expanding more on each of these areas at our Investor Day this coming March. With that, I'll turn it over to Jim to discuss more detailed financial information for the quarter and an update on our liquidity. Jim?
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Chris, and good morning, everyone. I'll now provide a comparison of our current quarter operating results versus the prior-year quarter and provide an update on our balance sheet and liquidity. Please refer to slide seven. Our net sales for the quarter ended 27 December 2024 increased approximately 8.7% to $1.034 billion from $950.5 million in Q4 2023. Net inflation was 3.8% in Q4, consisting of 5.1% inflation in our specialty category and inflation of 1.8% in our center of the plate category versus the prior-year quarter. Reported inflation was impacted by two primary factors in Q4 versus the prior-year quarter.
Prices in the chocolate category continued to remain elevated versus the prior year, and specialty product cross-sell growth in Texas. As we combine our legacy specialty and protein sales with our Hardie's produce operation, average revenue per case in Hardie's increased approximately 15% versus Q4 2023 as the mix of higher dollar specialty cases increased. Excluding the impact of the Texas cross-sell growth, aggregate specialty inflation was approximately 3.6%, and overall inflation for the company was approximately 3%. Gross profit increased 9.8% to $251 million for Q4 2024 versus $228.6 million for Q4 2023. Gross profit margins increased approximately 23 basis points to 24.3%.
Our procurement, sales, pricing, and operating teams delivered strong gross profit dollar growth across categories during the quarter. Selling, general, and administrative expenses increased approximately 8.9% to $206.8 million for Q4 2024 from $190 million for Q4 2023. The increase was primarily due to higher depreciation and amortization driven by facility investments and costs associated with compensation, facilities, and distribution to support sales growth. Adjusted operating expenses increased 7.7% versus the prior year Q4. As a percentage of net sales, adjusted operating expenses were 17.7% for Q4 2024. Operating income for Q4 2024 was $46.5 million, compared to $38.2 million for Q4 2023.
The increase in operating income was driven primarily by higher gross profit, partially offset by higher selling, general, and administrative expenses versus the prior-year quarter. Our GAAP net income was $23.9 million or $0.55 per diluted share for Q4 2024, compared to net income of $16 million or $0.38 per diluted share for Q4 2023. On a non-GAAP basis, we had Adjusted EBITDA of $68.2 million for Q4 2024, compared to $59 million for the prior-year Q4. Adjusted net income was $23.9 million or $0.55 per diluted share for Q4 2024, compared to $20.2 million or $0.47 per diluted share for the prior-year Q4.
Turning to the balance sheet and an update on our liquidity, please refer to slide eight. At the end of Q4, we had total liquidity of $261.4 million, comprised of $114.7 million in cash and $146.7 million of availability under our ABL facility. For the full fiscal year 2024, we prepaid $14 million principal on our 2029 term loan. We settled the December 2024 maturity convertible notes in a combination of cash and shares due to the partial conversion by certain holders. This resulted in $39.7 million of debt reduction and an increase in share count by 696,000 shares, net of 162,000 shares repurchased shortly following the conversion.
Share repurchases under our authorized $100 million plan totaled $17.4 million for the full year of 2024. Timing of any future repurchases under our plan will continue to be dependent on share price, market conditions, and free cash flow generation. As of 27 December, 2024, total net debt was approximately $557.8 million, net of all cash and cash equivalents. Net debt to Adjusted EBITDA was approximately 2.5x as compared to approximately 3.4x as of year-end 2023. Due to the timing of certain payments at year-end, we estimate that net debt to Adjusted EBITDA will be in the range of 2.5x to 2.8x for the foreseeable future. Turning to our full year guidance for 2025.
Based on the current trends in the business, we are providing our full year financial guidance as follows. We estimate that net sales for the full year of 2025 will be in the range of $3.94 to 4.04 billion. Gross profit to be between $951 and 976 million. Adjusted EBITDA to be between $233 and 246 million. Please note for the full year of 2025, we expect the convertible notes maturing in 2028 to be dilutive, and therefore we expect the fully diluted share count to be approximately 46.3 to 47 million shares. Thank you. At this point, we will open it up to questions. Operator?
Operator
Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star and one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star and two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. Ladies and gentlemen, we will wait for a moment while we poll for questions. The first question comes from the line of Mark Carden with UBS. Please go ahead.
Mark Carden
Director of Equity Research, UBS
Good morning. Thanks so much for taking the questions. To start, you guys called out strength across the quarter. Did you see any impact from the softer industry traffic that we've heard about in December? Or did the higher income consumer just simply act a bit differently? How much of an impact have you guys seen quarter to date from the southern winter storms and the California wildfires?
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Sorry, go ahead.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Go ahead.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
No, I would say that the cadence during Q4 was just pretty evenly solid or strong. I think, you know, a lot of people were anticipating maybe some impact from the shorter period from Thanksgiving to Christmas, but we really didn't see that. Those three weeks were really typically strong for a holiday season. There's really nothing to call out on Q4 in terms of weather impacts or any anything that we saw from a demand perspective. In terms of January and some of the weather impacts, you know, the fires in LA did not really have a hugely material impact on us. We only had a handful of customers that actually, you know, got lost their properties.
LA is a very big, wide market, geographically for us. There was a little bit of an impact, but it's not gonna have a material impact.
Mark Carden
Director of Equity Research, UBS
Great. That's helpful. Then in terms of, I know it's a fluid situation, but there's the potential for tariffs to come back into play with Mexico, Canada, and Europe. If that occurs, how much exposure do you have to these markets from an import perspective? Could you pass through the inflation in most cases, or would you look to pivot sourcing?
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I mean, historically, we went through a period of some tariff wars back years ago. I remember that, we were dealing with some of the products that, you know, come from Italy, France, and Spain, I believe. We have over 4,000 suppliers right now throughout our system at Chefs' Warehouse. A tremendous amount of our products are domestic. We've always been able to, you know, to navigate it, find other solutions, and pass on, you know. I mean, again, I think the, you know, the largest sector, I think, of the product lines are, you know, fruits and vegetables from Mexico. A lot of these are $20 boxes, so, you know, you're talking about a few bucks a case.
I think our market, our customer base is kind of used to the ups and downs. You know, we do sell a more high-end type of operation and, you know, it's more labor cost that drives a lot of the costs. I mean, right now everybody's talking about eggs. Eggs is, I think, the biggest headwind we have had from the avian flu. It's caused eggs to go up. When you really think about, you know, eggs are up—even if they're up $0.50 an egg, you know, how much of that goes into a recipe to our average customer who's charging $20, $30, $40 for an entree. There's an effect, but it's not something that really keeps me up at night.
Mark Carden
Director of Equity Research, UBS
Great. Thanks so much. Good luck, guys.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. The next question comes from Alex Slagle with Jefferies. Please go ahead.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Thanks. Hi, guys. Congrats on the quarter. Wanted to ask on the margin opportunities for 2025, and when you look at the implied midpoints for gross margin and OpEx, I mean, where do you think you see the greater opportunity to get more favorability? I ask that just because your adjusted OpEx percentage in Q4 2022 started to flatten out and leverage year-over-year for the first time in seven, eight quarters. From the outside, looks like a solid place to see some upside opportunity.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Curious on your perspective.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Thanks for the question, Alex. In terms of 2024, you know, we were pretty early upfront in our guidance that, you know, our operating leverage was gonna be heavily weighted to the back half of the year, especially Q4, given that we didn't lap some of the big facility investments and rent impacts until Q4. That kind of played out how we expected. We had very little operating leverage the first three quarters of the year and then a lot in Q4, and that resulted in the kind of 15 to 20 basis points of EBITDA margin improvement versus 2023. In 2025, you know, the guidance, you know, is obviously a range.
You know, our goal is once again to incrementally over the next four years, you know, improve operating leverage and EBITDA margin by, you know, kind of that 20 to 25 basis point range that we were close to executing in 2024. Really there's a lot of. You know, if you look at the chart that we put up about our 2028 financial goals, all of those things, you know, and the projects that are below them are all going into both driving gross profit dollar growth and improvement as well as improvement in adjusted operating leverage on the OpEx. You know, really it's just doing the work and the teams executing, and then getting there incrementally.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Okay. On the food cost inflation outlook, do you think that Hardie's cross-sell impact will continue through 2025 to the same degree?
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Well, I think we'll continue to grow the cross-sell. You know, with Hardie's it's similar to New England. We're trading out of some, you know, lower margin kind of what we call chunky corporate business and replacing it with what we call street sales, which are independent restaurants and the core customer that we're really good at serving. That will continue, and if it, you know, continues to have a bit of an outsized impact on the reported inflation number, you know, we'll call it out. You know, product mix changes impact the inflation versus volume number, and we'll continue to call things out that are having, you know, somewhat of an outsized impact one quarter versus another.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Unfortunately, Alex, I think that it makes your job a little harder trying to, you know, look at us over the past, you know, 10 years. I think we continue to say, to understand Chef, you have to understand our goal was to become a complete solution company in every market, you know. We have our protein offerings, and we have, now, our fresh offerings combined with the specialty broad line. You know, the numbers are gonna continue to evolve because our goal is to be, you know, that solution company in every market. It's gonna fluctuate, you know, depending if protein's growing faster than fresh or fresh is growing faster. It depends on the maturity of each market.
We're very, very happy with, you know, how our teams are growing, continually growing. We called it a hybrid selling for a long time. I think I'm gonna start maybe using a different phrase because, you know, maybe it's our total solution, go-to-market strategy that continues to evolve and succeed. I think that you're seeing the success of, how the teams are doing, you know, as we continue to get leverage on our overhead, you know, especially where we've invested heavily in people and technology, and on our new facilities. As we start to grow the volume, you start to see us get that leverage that we keep talking about, you know, 20 basis points a year for the next few years, and we're marching towards our goals.
Alex Slagle
Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Got it. Thanks. Congrats again.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Alex.
Operator
Thank you. The next question comes from the line of Peter Saleh with BTIG. Please go ahead.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director and Restaurants and Food Distributors Analyst, BTIG
Great. Thanks and congrats on a great year. I wanted to ask maybe first on just if you give us a little bit of an update. Chris, you mentioned labor costs, and maybe you could just give us an update on what you're thinking for labor availability and inflation in 2025, if you think that's gonna be in line with historical or outsized. Then just on general commodity inflation, I know in the past you've mentioned, you know, optimal scenario is 2% to 3% in commodity inflation with a little bit of volatility. Just any thoughts on what you're expecting in 2025 would be helpful. Then I've got a quick follow-up. Thanks.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Sure. Well, let me get the crystal ball out again, Peter. I think if you back out what we're seeing right now with you know, mainly, I mean, eggs is really what's got people going crazy at this point, you know. You know, the chocolate market is better, but it's still inflated. We back out those two big categories, we're kinda seeing that 2% to 3%, you know? I don't see anything you know, that really would change that drastically. I mean, everyone's talking about tariffs, but I don't know. From my seat today, I see the 2% to 3% that we talk about, you know, and probably with a little volatility.
We'll, you know, hopefully the egg market. You know, we get over the control of the avian flu and, you know, the egg prices start to come down, give people relief. Yeah, the meat market, I mean, we all talk about the beef, not enough cattle for the next two, three years, so I don't think we're gonna get much relief on that. We're seeing stabilization. We're not seeing, you know, we're not seeing anything crazy besides, you know, the big headwind on the egg market. You know, our category managers are really doing a great job right now, and I think you see the results.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director and Restaurants and Food Distributors Analyst, BTIG
Great. Just can I ask on the sales force? Can you give us an update on how, you know, the investments you guys have made in the sales force, maybe the growth rate? Where are you getting most of this talent from? Are they coming from outside the industry, within the industry? Any insight there would be helpful. Thank you.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Well, I didn't answer your labor question before. I mean, you know, labor, it's a hard job, you know, working night shifts and, you know, driving, you know, big trucks in cities and delivering it, you know, up and down stairs. I mean, these people work really hard. It's a hard job and, you know, we like to think we pay, you know, a very fair, you know, better than most of our competitors. We try to because we're delivering, you know, great expensive product to the best restaurants in the world. So, you know, we need to have the best team. I don't think that is the issue. It was obviously coming out of COVID, you know, where we were really challenged.
I think it's really stabilized. We have a stabilized labor force. I don't see that as the headwind that we had before. What was the second part of your question? I'm sorry, Peter. Oh, the sales force? Yeah. I mean, we hire from the kitchens, we hire from the front of the house, and we also hire people that have a passion for food, perseverance, and I think from all walks of life. You know, it's a very diverse sales force. I think it continues to get even more diverse.
I think what's really been paying us off dividends is our investments in training, you know, investments in HR, investments in recruiting, spending a lot of time, energy, and more and more investment in trying to recruit the best people because it does take time to become, I call it, you know, to become a real CW person who can sell all our books. That takes a few years. Hiring the wrong people who leave after a year or two is a big cash drain.
I think the efforts in making sure that we're doing our best to recruit people that are gonna stay, and I would say, you know, the people that stay more than two, three years, it becomes probably the best job, you know, that they're going to have because we don't cap people. We allow them to keep growing. I think that story resonates. They see the success, you know, people have had at Chefs' Warehouse, and I think that really helps us recruit the best people, best talent that's out there. I think you're seeing the results of that.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director and Restaurants and Food Distributors Analyst, BTIG
Thank you very much.
Operator
Thank you. The next question comes from Todd Brooks with The Benchmark Company. Please go ahead.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, The Benchmark Company
Hey, good morning, and congrats on a great 2024.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Todd.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, The Benchmark Company
A couple follow-up questions here. The strength that we saw in gross margin, you pointed to some specific drivers around the digital ordering mix, some beneficial inflationary experience, the higher kind of case value and profitability at Hardie's. As we're looking forward for gross margin outlook for 2025, just thoughts on kind of key drivers of continued improvement, and maybe if we can boil that into a magnitude, that would be great.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks for the question, Todd. I really go back to what I alluded to earlier, I guess, is that, you know, the guidance implies, you know, kind of very similar kind of gross profit margins, as we delivered in the full year of 2024. That's really because, you know, gross profit margins are an output and are affected by, you know, things like product mix changes, et cetera, as well as, you know, obviously inflation and deflation. You know, once again, we're focused on driving gross profit dollars and gross profit dollar growth. Texas is a good example.
As we get more expensive boxes on Hardie's trucks, you know, our goal is to drive more gross profit dollar per drop, per case average, and you know, for the OpCo as a whole as we go through the year. The operating team is focused on you know, managing operating expense. I think you know, when we build our guidance, we kinda just build in an expected gross profit range. It's not gonna, you know, be perfect. Our goal is to execute to you know, gross profit dollar growth. That's how we think about it.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. It's again, Todd. I think we've been saying, you know, focus on our spread between, you know, overhead, what it costs to run the business and the GP dollars because, you know, we're seeing a marketplace that didn't exist before in my 40 years in food service, where, you know, you have a case of eggs that was, say, $30 a case, and now it's $200 a case. You don't need to make, you know, 25%, right? 'Cause you're making the GP dollars because your input cost is so high. The overhead is up. It does cost, drivers cost more, rent costs more, but, you know, it didn't go up double and triple cost. You know, you're able to operate in this environment.
A case of prime filets, you know, that, say, was $80 a piece, and now it's $160 a piece. You have the same mathematical dynamic. The margin, you know, we are a margin company, we focus on it. But when you get crazy increases in certain categories, it can kinda muddle the number. Again, that's why we're so focused on saying, you know, our focus is delivering that 20 basis point improvement, you know, every year. It's really the spread between the operating cost to run the business and the GP dollars coming in because our mixes are changing. You know, we are a company that's focused on selling, you know, the best products in the world.
A lot of them are more expensive. Our customers use more expensive ingredients. So it's not like we're stuck with a $20 box type of food distribution business and trying to make a $1.95 a case. That's not who Chefs' Warehouse is. That's why we give up, you know, sometimes $50, $60, $70, $100 million of volume that comes in from some of these acquisitions that doesn't fit who we are. As we kinda right-size the market, as we talk about Texas, it starts to become more of a Chefs' Warehouse, and it starts to look and operate more like a Chefs' Warehouse, and the numbers start to become more like a Chefs' Warehouse.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, The Benchmark Company
That's very helpful. Thanks, Chris. Just one quick follow-up with inflation being kind of a key topic on this call. How are you guys looking about potential issues as you go down the supply chain from labor availability, whether it's migrant labor on the produce side of the business or maybe labor on the meat processing and packaging side as an incremental pressure to inflation in your 2025 outlook? Thanks.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I think we got way ahead of it the past few years. I mean, we raised a lot of the wages, you know. I think that we realized to get the best talent out there, we would have to pay, you know, in each market, you know, to be most competitive, to look for the best people. Again, you know, be successful, you can afford to pay more, right? I think we're doing that. I'm not sure that we're going to see, you know, a tremendous headwind coming from the labor front because we're already paying, I think, you know, at the upper end of the market.
I think to attract, to keep attracting that talent, I think it's built into our market. I think we're good there.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Todd, I would just add that on the processing side, you know, given the facility investments that we've made over the last couple of years, we put in a lot of processing automation, and that's allowed us to, you know, to hire fewer butchers. That'll help mitigate as well as we go forward.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. All our systems in the warehouse is making us more efficient. You know, we know that that's the key to the success going forward is, you know, you have to be able to figure out how to do more with less, and I think our teams are doing a phenomenal job of that.
Todd Brooks
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, The Benchmark Company
Okay, great. Thank you both.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Todd.
Operator
Thank you. The next question comes from the line of Elle Niebuhr with Lake Street Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
Elle Niebuhr
Equity Research Associate, Lake Street Capital Markets
Hey guys, this is Elle on for Ben Klieve. Congrats on a strong quarter, and thanks for taking my questions. First, could you provide an update on the utilization levels in the new Texas, California, and Florida locations? How do these compare to your initial expectations, and are you seeing any regional trends going forward?
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Well, we don't—Thanks for the question, Elle. We don't really disclose utilization levels by operating company or by market. In general, you know, in Northern California, we completed the consolidation of four processing facilities into one. We completed that move in December 2024, and we're in the early innings of that operation. That is really exciting. I mean, we have a lot of room for growth in that facility, and we're starting to realize the benefits of removing four separate processing facilities and getting the synergies on the operating cost side. In Texas, you know, we've taken some additional space in Houston.
We're in the process of, as I mentioned earlier, and Chris mentioned earlier as well, trading out of some non-core business that will free up space in order to continue to grow the specialty and protein side of the business, selling to the large Hardie's customer base that we acquired with the acquisition. Getting those routes was critical to that part of the strategy. We're doing that in a number of different markets, maybe on different levels of scale, but hopefully that gives you a sense of where we are, you know, in a multi-year path to driving the improvements in those markets from those investments.
Elle Niebuhr
Equity Research Associate, Lake Street Capital Markets
Yeah, that's great. Thanks. A second question, and then I'll hop back in queue. Could you break down your CapEx expectations for this year in terms of growth versus maintenance spending? How should we think about your capital allocation strategy between expansion initiatives and sustaining existing operations?
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah, sure. So we guided, you know, to CapEx of $40 to 50 million for 2025, very similar to what we're doing in 2024. You know, our goal is to gradually get that down towards 1% of revenue. I think we'll be closer to that versus I think we were at 1.3% in 2024. In general, because we're a growth company, 80% of our CapEx is basically investing in facility expansion. We have two major projects that we're doing in 2025, and that is our Philadelphia, Southern New Jersey facility retrofit that will optimize our distribution footprint between the New York Metro area, the Mid-Atlantic, and Pennsylvania. That's underway.
Our Portland, Oregon, facility build out that will allow us to consolidate multiple facilities that we have in Portland as a result of an acquisition that we did over a couple of years ago. That's taking place this year as well. We anticipate to complete that either at the end of this year or early Q1 of 2026. Those are the two major facility projects, and really the rest of our CapEx is investments in technology, in our digital platform build out, and then the rest is maintenance CapEx.
Elle Niebuhr
Equity Research Associate, Lake Street Capital Markets
That's great. Thanks, guys. That's it for me.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Kelly Bania with BMO Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
Kelly Bania
Managing Director of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Good morning. Thanks for taking our questions. Was wondering if you could just talk a little bit more about the 4% to 7% organic growth, and just help us break that down between how much high growth markets are contributing versus more mature markets. Obviously tie in Texas into that conversation and just what you're learning about the Texas market and the receptivity to the categories as you integrate kind of protein and specialty there.
James Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Kelly. I'll start with a little bit about the high growth markets and the mature markets, and then I'll turn it over to Chris to add some color on Texas and the strategy there. Just on the 4% to 7%, you know, we have, and we'll talk more about this at our Investor Day. We have, you know, markets like Dubai, Florida, and Seattle, even Southern California, Northern California, Texas, and New England, where we've made, you know, either significant acquisitions that are aimed at growth and invested in capacity. All of these markets that I'm mentioning are kind of in that group.
They're growing. I'm not gonna call out specific markets, but you know, most of them are growing double digits, you know, anywhere between 10% and 20%. Our mature markets are still growing, but obviously if you're in a market like San Francisco or LA or where we've been a long time, it's a very big market. We're growing through category growth. We're growing through, you know, penetration and continuing to add customers in the outlying markets where people are working, given hybrid work, et cetera. Many of those dynamics are still playing out. They're still growing, you know, mid-single digits or, you know, that kind of type of growth. I hope, Kelly, that frames-
Kind of the 4% to 7% growth, and then I'll ask Chris to just comment on your comment on Texas and the strategy there.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Thanks, Kelly. Yeah, I mean, Texas again, I mean, it's gonna be a top three market. Yeah, you have to look at it over the next four or five years. I mean, you know, we've been through this drill before where we acquire some businesses. They're not exactly what we call Chefs' Warehouse, and it takes time to get the buildings right and the technology and the mix and train the salespeople. So, couldn't be prouder of our team in Texas and all they've accomplished, you know, trying to create, you know, the Chefs' Warehouse formula. I think it's gonna be a little bit at a time, and then you get that giant waterfall like we've done in a lot of other markets where we do get everything aligned.
We get, we build the sales force that's trained, understands all the categories. We get the customers that we're really looking for that fit who CW is right. We off-board, not purposely, but there's a lot of business that, you know, comes with some of these acquisitions that's really better served by maybe a chain distributor. That's not what we really focus on, and we really build that, you know, the independents, the small groups. Texas is just booming with, you know, the culinary scene that's, you know, more typical of New York and San Francisco, LA, Chicago. A lot of our operators are opening up in Texas, and that's why we were so excited to get in that market. We're just being patient now, you know, what we call transformation.
We've bought, you know, some really great businesses, but you know, to making them into a Chefs' Warehouse, you know, takes some time, and I think right now they're probably in the second inning. You know, I think we got through the first. We're making great headway, and that team is just gonna continue to march over the next four or five years. Then, you know, looking further out, I think it starts to look more and more like New York, and that's really our goal.
Kelly Bania
Managing Director of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Very, very helpful. Just another follow-up. I think the slide deck mentioned 56% of specialty customers ordering via digital. Just wondering if we could talk about that a little bit more. Are your smaller kinda specialty competitors really ramping with this type of service? And just how is this favorably impacting gross margin and gross profit growth? And where do you see that penetration of digital going kind of over time?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah, I mean, I think that over time, 80%, 90% of the customers are not gonna pick up the phone, right? It's email, it's text, and then it's using our online capabilities. As we get better and better, as that team continues to build, I think we have tremendous upside still in improving our website and improving our capabilities, even though we've come a long, long way. It just creates a more dynamic addition to dealing, you know, with Chefs' Warehouse. You know, we have over 55,000, you know, in some markets, 80,000 items that go through the system. It's just such a great tool to support the sales team, you know.
I think you've heard me say for a while now, you know, the sales force of the future are consultants. You know, they don't have to do what they did years ago. You know, be stuck at their computer waiting to take orders. I mean, I remember when we started the company, it was paper and pencil, right? Laptops were great. You know, they freed up salespeople. They can go on the road and then pull over, and when they got Wi-Fi, they can take orders from the road, from hotels. Now that I think the next big jump is, the customers are placing their orders. Salespeople are checking in, referring items, suggesting, you know, they're becoming solution, more solution type of, consultants.
As that continues, sales, the customers are finding more items online that they didn't know we carry, or they're changing menus, and they're searching. That's where really our strength is. You know, we have the long tail. We have so many different types of gourmet items and solution items, and I think that's what's helping, you know, the margins. I think that's helping placements. We saw, you know, in a year that all we heard about was, you know, the headwinds of the restaurant industry. Customer counts were down, people were spending a little less. We had a tremendous year, I think because of the tools we've added and of all the training and the salespeople were aligned with us.
I think that's just gonna continue now, and we haven't even really implemented into our protein divisions in some of our new companies. I think we have tremendous upside, you know, as we continue to mature.
Kelly Bania
Managing Director of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Thank you.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Kelly.
Operator
Thank you. The next question comes from the line of Andrew Wolf with C.L. King. Please go ahead.
Andrew Wolf
SVP and Senior Research Analyst, C.L. King & Associates
Thanks. Good morning. Wanted to on the deck where you referenced the increase in EBITDA per employee, you know, really a big jump last year, 13% year-over-year increase. You know, I think, Chris, you referenced better training, HR practices, and so on, but could you give us a little more color? Is that more on the gross profit line, you were to break it down or more on the operating leverage line? You know, is there sort of a bit of some catch up in there from sort of the COVID impact on productivity, and you know, people are finally learning their jobs, and there's a big productivity surge. What I'm really getting to is, you know, is this something that is sustainable?
Is it gonna be a much better, you know, as you guys look at the business through 2028, much better type of, you know, employee productivity, on the profit side, I would imagine on the sales side as well?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I'll start with the first part of your question, Andy. The 13% is really—it's really, really aligned with our overall EBITDA and operating leverage improvement 2024 over 2023. As I mentioned earlier, it was a little uneven, with a lot of that leverage coming in the Q4. That's really driven by, you know, the cadence of the facility investments and when we lap them. Yeah, from a productivity perspective, I think our teams did a great job of managing headcount and managing operating spend throughout the year. That shows up in the productivity that we, you know, that you're talking about on the chart. It came from both gross profit dollar growth and margin improvement.
As I mentioned, sometimes you'll get gross profit dollar growth, with, you know, minimal margin improvement because you're selling more expensive boxes or you're driving the product mix that Chris talked about with, different markets like Texas, et cetera. It's really just comes from, you know, from that, our teams executing on that strategy. I'm sorry, the last part of your question was?
Andrew Wolf
SVP and Senior Research Analyst, C.L. King & Associates
Oh, just the outlook. I mean, your EBITDA is up 13%. The EBITDA per headcount is up 13%. You know, just sort of back of the envelope, it implies you didn't add net new headcount. I can't imagine that's the plan. You know, is it gonna be something like it moderates to 10% a year? I mean, I'm just. I'm not asking, I don't know if you want to share that number, but just a sense of, I mean, this is a big improvement, and you know, what the go-forward look is like.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Andy, I think you gotta look at. I mean, I know it's hard for you guys to model, but it's kind of a Goldilocks. It's a little bit of everything. I think you have to remember that, you know, we went from $300 million to a $4 billion company in the last 10 years. We've, you know, we've taken some hits, right? The stock's gone up and down, and I think people maybe misunderstood how well we were doing because the numbers weren't always the numbers the Street wanted to see because we were buying companies for the right price, and we had to transform them. The great thing about Chefs' Warehouse is there's really nobody like us.
The bad thing is there's no one exactly like us to buy. So we have to buy companies, and we have to transform them as Chefs. We, you know, we made that big leap. So, you know, we're in a much different position now than we were 12 years ago. Sure, we wanna be acquisitive, we wanna take advantage of opportunities, but, you know, we built, you know, I don't know, 30, 40 warehouses. We've hired thousands of people. All that took time, a lot of training. We had to implement systems. We had to transform systems. Now you're starting to see more production. I mean, we expect that, right? We made the investment.
As people get better, you know, more highly trained, like in any industry, you know, you go up the ladder, you know, you get your bachelor's and maybe your master's and your PhD, and now you're becoming an expert in your field. That's why we don't wanna train people that don't stay. I think it's a lot of investment in everything, and we're starting to reap those rewards. Of course, you know, you hit a hurricane, everybody's numbers go backwards.
you know, right now in a very tough market where, you know, there's competition everywhere for restaurants and, you know, maybe headcounts are down some and a little spend, the only way to put up the numbers we're putting up is by taking market share, and I think our team is doing a great job.
Andrew Wolf
SVP and Senior Research Analyst, C.L. King & Associates
Thank you. I got that. Just one final one, if I may. You know, these integrated, you know, big distribution centers that you just put one up in Northern California. You know, I think, I don't know if Florida is the longest tenured one, but could you give us a sense of the, you know, they may not be mature yet, but how they're performing, you know, the ones that have been open a while, to either boost sales with more cross-sell, just expanding the market with capacity, and how the capital returns are looking. I know it's early stages for most of them.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I mean, the newest ones, I think, you know, we've been announcing, you know, Florida's actually, I think we've only been in there. I don't even know if it's two years, right? They're doing great. You know, we're really proud of them, and we think they're firing on all pistons, and that's Florida's gonna be such a great market for us. You know, LA, I mean, that's a pretty new facility. You know, that facility was built to quadruple the business. We have lots of capacity. They're doing great, so we're really excited about their future.
The latest one to open was really a processing facility that Jim referred to earlier, that we consolidated a bunch of facilities we had in Northern California into, one of the most state-of-the-art processing facilities in the country. We're really excited about, you know, they went through a lot. I mean, to consolidate those many facilities is a lot of work. They were very distracted. I think it was a really rough time the last few years, and now they can really focus on growth again. You know, now that they're under one roof, I'm sure there's other markets we've entered that, you know, we're still in the first inning, you know, small outposts that we developed, you know, going south into Tennessee and into Detroit. You know, we've kinda slowed it down for everybody to catch up.
You know, we have some new facilities. New England's gonna need a new facility. They're operating out of multiple buildings, so we've seen that movie before. We just opened up, you know, what we call our Pennsylvania South Jersey facility. It's not completed, but we're really excited about that. A lot of exciting things going on.
Andrew Wolf
SVP and Senior Research Analyst, C.L. King & Associates
Okay. Thank you for the call. Appreciate it.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Andy.
Operator
Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, as there are no further questions, I would now like to hand the conference over to Chris Pappas for closing comments.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Sure. Well, we thank everybody for joining our call today. I think we're very proud of what the CW family of companies has accomplished in 2024, and we're looking forward to a great 2025 and beyond. We're looking forward to everyone joining our next earnings call. Thank you very much.
Operator
Thank you. The conference of The Chefs' Warehouse has now concluded. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect your lines. Thank you.

Operator
Greetings, and welcome to the Chefs' Warehouse Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your host, Alex Aldous, General Counsel, Corporate Secretary, and Chief Government Relations Officer. Please go ahead, sir.
Alex Aldous
General Counsel, Corporate Secretary, and Chief Government Relations Officer, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone. With me on today's call are Chris Pappas, Founder, Chairman, and CEO, and Jim Leddy, our CFO. By now, you should have access to our Q2 2024 earnings press release. It can also be found at www.chefswarehouse.com under the Investor Relations section. Throughout this conference call, we will be presenting non-GAAP financial measures, including, among others, historical and estimated EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA, as well as both historical and estimated adjusted net income and adjusted earnings per share. These measurements are not calculated in accordance with GAAP and may be calculated differently in similarly titled non-GAAP financial measures used by other companies. Quantitative reconciliations of our non-GAAP financial measures to their most directly comparable GAAP financial measures appear in today's press release.
Before we begin our formal remarks, I need to remind everyone that part of our discussion today will include forward-looking statements, including statements regarding our estimated financial performance. Such forward-looking statements are not guarantees of future performance, and therefore, you should not put undue reliance on them. These statements are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from what we expect. Some of these risks are mentioned in today's release. Others are discussed in our annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, which are available on the SEC website. Today, we are going to provide a business update and go over our Q2 results in detail. Then we will open up the call for questions. With that, I will turn the call over to Chris Pappas. Chris.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Alex, and thank you all for joining our Q2 2024 earnings call. Q2 customer demand and pricing displayed typical seasonality as revenue and profitability continued to build as expected, moving from a solid Q1 into seasonally stronger Q2 months. Our operating divisions across domestic and international markets delivered strong, unique customer and item placement growth and managed pricing effectively while providing our customers with high-quality product and high-value service. We are extremely proud of all our teams from sales, sourcing, pricing, operations, and support functions coming together to deliver value to our customers, leveraging our diverse and broad supply chain, value-add processing, and culinary expertise to assist our customers with managing menu development as well as product and labor-related costs. A few highlights from Q2 include 7.2% organic growth in net sales.
Specialty sales were up 7.5% organically over the prior year, which was driven by unique customer growth of approximately 8.2%, placement growth of 11.3%, and specialty case growth of 4.7%. Excluding prior year low-margin customer attrition in Hardie's, total specialty cases grew approximately 5.5% year-over-year in Q2. Organic pounds in center of the plate were approximately 2.9% higher than the prior year Q2. Gross profit margins increased approximately 35 basis points. Gross margin in the specialty category increased approximately 50 basis points as compared to Q2 2023, while gross margin in the center of the plate category were essentially flat year-over-year.
Jim will provide more detail on gross profit and margins in a few moments. We remain focused on making progress towards our five-year goals, which include 2028 revenue of approximately $4.6 billion to $5 billion, and adjusted EBITDA of $300 to $350 million. It is important to highlight the key investments we have put in place to provide our teams with the market footprint, product categories, infrastructure, and investment, and sales force necessary to grow towards achieving these targets. Regarding infrastructure, since 2019, we have added approximately 1 million sq ft of distribution capacity, excluding acquisitions, or approximately a 60% increase to the 2019 baseline. These include investments in future growth in high value markets, such as the expansion of our distribution centers in Dubai, Seattle, Southern California, and Florida.
This also includes facility expansion to create future operating synergies, such as our recently completed protein processing facility in Northern California. During Q2, we initiated processing operations and completed the first phase of a multiple facility consolidation with the move of our Brisbane processing and distribution operation. We expect to complete the next move during Q3, with the focus on completing the full consolidation during Q1 2025. We expect to provide route, labor, and technology-driven efficiencies with room for future growth in the region. Regarding our investments in sales and our unique go-to-market strategy since year-end 2021, we have increased our sales force, excluding acquisitions, by approximately 10% per year.
Over the same time frame, in certain of our high growth investment markets, such as Florida, the Middle East, and California, we have grown our sales force by approximately 20 to 25% per year on average. In addition, we continue to invest in category expertise in digital and pricing tools across our markets to support our sales and operating teams' execution in growing market share via unique item penetration, new customer acquisition, and improved gross profit dollars per delivery. Our investments in acquisitions, categories, infrastructure, and sales teams have given us the marketing and distribution footprint required for growth towards our 2028 goals. We feel we have a balanced portfolio of high growth markets supported by ample capacity, maturing sales teams with our unique go-to-market strategy, complemented by more mature markets focused on category expansion and continued above average industry growth.
For the past 40 years, we have developed a moat in our niche of the food service industry by investing in and developing the talent and expertise to sell to the world's finest chefs, to be logistically nimble and best in class to manage just-in-time service, and to manage price and margins in a volatile world. We have built a culture and strategy designed to be the unique food service solution company focused on serving quality culinary-driven operators. With that, I'll turn it over to Jim to discuss more detailed financial information for the quarter and an update on our liquidity. Jim?
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thank you, Chris, and good morning, everyone. I'll now provide a comparison of our current quarter operating results versus the prior year quarter and provide an update on our balance sheet and liquidity. Our net sales for the quarter ended 28 June 2024 increased approximately 8.3% to $954.7 million, from $881.8 million in Q2 2023. The growth in net sales was a result of an increase in organic sales of approximately 7.2%, as well as the contribution of sales from acquisitions, which added approximately 1.1% to sales growth for the quarter.
Net inflation was 3.3% in Q2, consisting of 2.7% inflation in our specialty category and inflation of 4.3% in our center of the plate category versus the prior year quarter. Gross profit increased 9.9% to $229 million for Q2 of 2024 versus $208.4 million for Q2 of 2023. Gross profit margins increased approximately 35 basis points to 24%, and our procurement, sales, pricing, and operating teams delivered strong gross profit dollar growth across categories during the quarter. Selling, general, and administrative expenses increased approximately 8.8% to $194.8 million for Q2 of 2024, from $179 million for Q2 of 2023.
The increase was primarily due to higher depreciation and amortization, driven by acquisitions and facility investments, and costs associated with compensation, facility costs, and distribution costs to support sales growth in the current quarter. Adjusted operating expenses increased 9.8% versus the prior year's Q2. As a percentage of net sales, adjusted operating expenses were 18.1% for Q2 2024. Operating income for Q2 2024 was $33.9 million, compared to $25.3 million for Q2 2023. The increase in operating income was driven primarily by higher gross profit, partially offset by higher selling, general, and administrative expenses versus the prior year quarter.
Income tax expense was $6.7 million for Q2 2024, compared to $3.5 million expense for Q2 2023. Our GAAP net income was $15.5 million or $0.37 per diluted share for Q2 2024, compared to net income of $9.9 million or $0.25 per diluted share for Q2 2023. On a non-GAAP basis, we had adjusted EBITDA of $56.2 million for Q2 2024, compared to $51.1 million for the prior year's Q2. Adjusted net income was $17 million or $0.40 per diluted share for Q2 2024, compared to $14.4 million or $0.35 per diluted share for the prior year's Q2.
Turning to the balance sheet and an update on our liquidity. At the end of Q2, we had total liquidity of $208.3 million, comprised of $38.3 million in cash and $170 million of availability under our ABL facility. During Q2, we continued to make progress toward achieving our year-end 2025 capital allocation goals of 2.5 to 3x net debt leverage and repurchasing $25 million to $100 million of equivalent outstanding shares. As of 28 June 2024, year to date, we have repurchased $10 million of our outstanding common shares, resulting in a reduction of approximately 264,000 shares outstanding and repaid $14.5 million of outstanding debt.
June 2024, total net debt was approximately $661 million, inclusive of all cash and cash equivalents, and net debt to adjusted EBITDA was approximately 3.2x as compared to approximately 3.3x as of Q1 2024. Turning to our full year guidance for 2024. Based on the current trends in the business, we are providing our full year financial guidance as follows. We estimate that net sales for the full year of 2024 will be in the range of $3.665 billion to $3.785 billion. Gross profit to be between $874 million and $902 million. Adjusted EBITDA to be between $208 million and $219 million.
Please note, for the Q3 of 2024, we expect both convertible notes maturing in December of this year and those maturing in 2028 to be diluted for reporting purposes, and therefore, we expect the fully diluted share count to be approximately 45.9 million shares. For the Q4 and for the full year of 2024, we expect the remaining convertible notes maturing in 2028 to be diluted, and therefore, we expect the fully diluted share count to be approximately 45 million shares for the Q4 and full year reporting periods. Operator

The first question we have is from Alex Slagle of Jefferies. Please go ahead.
Alex Slagle
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Thanks. Good morning. Hey, guys. Wanted to ask on the case growth opportunity for the H2, and maybe if you could just talk to some of the drivers and pipeline visibility you have that kinda give you confidence being able to continue driving the organic case growth like you have recently. I know consumer demand in the restaurant industry more broadly seems to have gotten a little bit choppier, so just wanted to get kinda your thoughts and things that give you confidence in the H2.
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Sure. Yeah. Andy, I mean, again, I think that our clientele, you know, had a pretty strong Q2. I think when you look at last year as well, you know, as you came into the summertime, you know, it was a little choppy last year. I think, you know, it's too early to see, but I think it's kind of, you know, becoming more of a typical summer where, you know, a lot of people from the US travel, and last year, you know, we saw it, like, come roaring back again in September.
You know, forecasting, you know, we're looking at bookings, we're looking at hotel bookings, we're looking at conferences, we're looking at corporate events, we're looking at, you know, talking to our customers. You know, we see a pretty normal type of Q3, Q4 last year, you know, hopefully coming together. We've invested so much in, you know, what we call the hybrid sale. We've put lots of teams out there. We're cross-selling. We're putting more and more, you know, trained salespeople out in the street. We've added the capacity in the warehouses. I think it's what we're expecting.
You know, we've invested in it and, you know, obviously, it could be up or down a little bit, but, you know, we feel pretty good about, you know, where we've invested and, boots on the ground and our product mix, which I think is the most unique in the industry. We continue to see, you know, new openings, and I think, that's where we're winning a lot. You know, I always say restaurateurs open restaurants. People that, you know, are in the hotel business wanna build hotels.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
I think what you're seeing more and more is, you know, I'm reading some of the reports where headcounts are down in restaurants, you know, 2% to 3% depending on your sector. We also have so many openings. I think where Chef is winning is we're winning in the openings, and that could be making up for any sort of headwinds in customer counts.
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Alex, you know, I'll just add that, you know, we're reporting H1, you know, new customer acquisition, you know, close to 10%, just under 10%. Item placement growth, double digits, 11% to 12%. That's been making up for, you know, a little bit of the moderation that, you know, Chris mentioned that you're seeing in terms of, you know, demand or volume and especially during the summer. Some of the investments that we've made, in those areas, in category growth, in sales force, and some of the tools we're giving them are paying off.
Alex Slagle
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Got it. Jim, a follow-up, if you could provide any color around potential cadence of the margin leverage we have in the H2. I know the 3Q laps, there are some unique headwinds and some timing dynamics at play as you roll off, like the increased demand from some of the new facilities and all.
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. The guidance, you know, the guidance implies, obviously in the H1, organic growth was closer to 8%, but the full year guidance implies kind of 6% to 7% organic revenue growth. We had already built in a deceleration, a moderate deceleration in the H2 in terms of organic revenue growth. That's really driven by the comparisons, because if you remember last summer, we really had a margin issue driven by the protein markets. It wasn't a volume issue. We had really good year-over-year, you know, volume and revenue growth. We're comping to a little bit of a tougher comp in the H2, but that's really just driven by last year's cadence versus this year.
Alex Slagle
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Jefferies
Okay. Thanks for the help.
Operator
The next question we have is from Mark Carden of UBS. Please go ahead.
Mark Carden
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Good morning. Thanks so much for taking the question. I want to dig in a bit more on sales. Sounds like your customers are holding up pretty well overall. I know last quarter you talked about some pressure at some of your casual customers. Has it remained pretty constrained, this customer segment, or are you seeing it creep into a broader swath of your customers' restaurants?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I'm trying to recall really what you're referencing to, but you know, again, our customer base is extremely diverse. You know, we purposely hire trained large teams to go after different types of business, caterers, upscale, fast casual, you know, hotels, cruise ships, all the way up to you know, what I call super fine dining. You know, we purposely have the diverse clientele to kind of balance out you know, anything that you know, any headwinds in certain sectors. As you can see, you know, Q2 was pretty good.
You know, we felt our customer base, you know, did pretty well, you know, in an environment that, you know, we see a lot of the numbers coming out of, you know, QSR and some of the lower priced restaurant groups. We think our customers are pretty savvy. They understand how to, you know, where they have to promote, give a little bit more value. On the higher end, I think it's bifurcated. You know, you have certain sectors that have slowed down a little bit.
You know, you see a lot of the reports coming out of other distributors and the restaurant reports, and other parts of our clientele have accelerated. I think that balanced attack, you know, is helping us, you know, put up pretty good numbers.
Mark Carden
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Great. Inflation appears to be pretty healthy. Any unusual dynamics to call out on that front? Just how are you thinking about it now for the balance of the year?
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Not really anything to call out. I mean, you look at Q1 and Q2 together, you know, roughly 3% type of average inflation. I would say there's a couple of categories on the specialty side that are, you know, driving probably the difference between kinda 2% and 3%. I mean, I think everybody's aware of, you know, what's happened with olive oil and some categories like chocolate, you know, driven by weather in different parts of the world. Excluding those, you're kind of in that normal kinda 2% to 3% range. We don't really expect anything materially different at this point going forward.
Mark Carden
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Great. Thanks so much, and good luck, guys.
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks.
Operator
The next question we have is from Todd Brooks of The Benchmark Company. Please go ahead.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Hey, Todd.
Todd Brooks
Equity Research Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Hey, guys. Good morning. Congrats on the results in the quarter. Couple quick questions for you. If you look across your customer base, just wondering what you're seeing as far as geographic disparities in performance. If you look at the California market, I don't know if some of that angst that we're hearing about broadly in the category has crept into the fine dining end of the sector there. We also hear that Florida remains a challenged market. Just wondering if you look across the base, maybe strong versus weaker markets and thoughts on that.
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
We haven't really seen a huge disparity across regions. I think, you know, we've mentioned on our Q1 call that, you know, we saw some of the higher-end steakhouses are down, you know, year-over-year from a traffic perspective, or there's a bit of a trade-down where, you know, we're selling more high-end burgers versus the, maybe the prime steaks, but we're still making good margin on those. We see different dynamics across, you know, our regions. Our international markets are doing really well. There's a number of domestic markets that are showing strength. Some are showing a little bit more moderation. I don't think there's any specific markets that we would call out as being significantly different.
I would just say that there's, you know, pockets of moderation across regions.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I mean, I'll add a little more color to that. I think that you know where there is a little bit of softness, I think in everybody reporting in the same-store sales, I think we're seeing the same thing in you know we're adding so many customers in Southern California where we've you know added you know a state-of-the-art facility and more boots on the ground. I think it's the same in Florida. You know, Florida had great numbers for us. You know, they continue to grow. You know, we started off pretty small.
You know, we just opened up our new facility. I think any sort of softness in same-store sales, you know, we're optimistic that we're making it up because we are, you know, we are winning and we're adding, you know, continuing to add, you know, customers daily. I think it's because of our size too. You know, we're relatively small, I think, to the major players that we're in Florida. I think that, you know, the Chefs' go-to-market strategy, who we are, what we're selling, is making up for any of that softness. You know, I think we've seen this in our past so many years in business.
You know, it's really a pattern that, you know, we've done pretty well, even when there's some headwinds and some softness, you know, in the consumer.
Todd Brooks
Equity Research Analyst, The Benchmark Company
That's great. My second question, and Jim, you pointed to the international markets doing very well. Can you just remind us on the distribution facility expansion timing for CME and give maybe a sense of what the old facility could handle capacity-wise and what it should be able to handle post the expansion being done? Thanks.
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah, thanks for the question, Todd. We're doubling the size of the facility. They were actually using a lot of kind of off-campus storage and freezer space, which was fairly expensive. We'll finish that project probably at the end of Q3, early Q4, and then do a kind of phased move through Q4. We'll see most of the growth and benefits really coming into 2025 and into 2026. Yeah, we're going from about 100,000 sq ft to 200,000 sq ft with a lot of room for growth. That market is growing. It's very dynamic. We're pretty excited about it.
Even in their current space, they've been doing really well as they continue to grow in that market.
Todd Brooks
Equity Research Analyst, The Benchmark Company
Okay, great. Thanks, guys.
Jim Leddy
CFO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks.
Operator
The next question we have is from Peter Saleh of BTIG. Please go ahead.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, BTIG
Great. Thanks, and congrats on the quarter. I did wanna ask, it sounds like you guys are continuing to win with new restaurant openings and new restaurant formation. I think you mentioned new customer acquisitions up about 10%. Is there any reason to believe that new restaurant formation will slow or that this trend will slow at all over the coming years? Is there anything that leads you to believe that this trend won't continue?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah, great question. You know, if I had the crystal ball, I'd feel a little bit better. You know, again, I could just go about our history and, you know, the world's changed since COVID. I think I remember, you know, even coming out of COVID, I said there's gonna be an acceleration of openings because they were delayed, right, during COVID. You know, you see a lot of change in cities. You know, you see the real estate dynamics of, you know, trying to reinvent buildings that were offices and, you know, trying to change those neighborhoods into more, you know, where they can add housing. You know, we see a change in the suburbs, where people are working more from home, you know, a few days a week.
I think restaurateurs, you know, continue to follow the money, and they continue to open restaurants where the traffic patterns, you know, seem to be, especially, you know, with real estate developers, a lot of them, you know, building restaurants to attract people to those areas, Peter. I don't think I'm gonna see much of a slowdown. I think a lot of, you know, the restaurant world is trying to reinvent itself, too, in a change. You know, there's more takeout, there's more. You know, what we have seen is a proliferation of different types of restaurants and different types of food away from home. You know, I mean, I continue to believe that people really are too busy to wanna cook.
You know, even when they're going to the markets, they're buying a lot of prepared foods. I think more and more of our great chefs, restauranteurs are getting more and more into that business. I think that's, you know, making up for maybe where there's softness in the typical sit-down restaurants that people are used to. The other side of that business has accelerated, and it's, you know, better food that you could take out or get delivered, or it's food that, you know, you could sit down and eat or you could take it home. You know, we're seeing a tremendous proliferation of new types of outlets for us to sell.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, BTIG
Great. Then just on the investment in the sales team, you know, 10% annual sales growth or sales team growth over the past several years. You know, giving your targets into 2028, are you anticipating to accelerate that or keep that kind of pace of investment in the sales team the same?
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I mean, I think the pace is, you know, what we budgeted and forecasted to spend. You know, we're looking at the dynamics of our business. You know, there's been so much talk about, you know, online will replace salespeople, which we think online is making salespeople more efficient and giving them more time to do what we really want them to do, is be consultants. I think I've been beating that drum for the last four or five years that, you know, the crystal ball says that, you know, online is gonna get better and better.
You know, younger people, as they come into the industry, are gonna use a lot of those tools 'cause they're so used to, you know, being on an app and researching. We, you know, are investing in better information, more information online, being a partner to our customer, assisting them in menu development, assisting them in. You know, chefs are curious. You know, they're constantly, you know, wanting to learn and constantly wanting to invent. We're trying to, you know, be that partner that's supplying that information. Again, we continue to add people because we see that, you know, for what we do, and it might not work for everybody's business, they wanna see somebody who, you know, is talking to them.
We have, you know, a tremendous amount of talent that, you know, mans the phone still. Obviously, we could chat if you wanna be just online. We like to give our customers choices, and we think that, you know, we found a winning balance for now, it can always change, that really works for our customers, and it's driving, you know, more volume to all our chef customers, all our chef opcos.
Peter Saleh
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, BTIG
Thank you very much.
Operator
The next question we have is from Kelly Bania of BMO Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
Ben Wood
Vice President of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Hi, good morning. This is Ben Wood on for Kelly. Thank you for taking our questions. First, we just wanted to dig in a little bit more on the unique customer growth and the placement growth. Are there specific regions or markets that are driving that, or is that fairly consistent throughout your markets? Just hoping you can help us frame how maybe high growth markets are comparing to your mature markets, and if those high growth areas you're investing in, how they are tracking against your expectations.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. Thanks for the question, Ben. Yeah, we always have, you know, like Chris mentioned in his prepared remarks, we always have in our portfolio, you know, a mix of more mature markets, you know, like the Northeast and other areas that, you know, we've been operating for 40 years. Then our newer higher growth investment markets that we've talked about, you know, as we're coming out of our heavy investment cycle, like Florida and Southern California, Dubai, Seattle, some of our smaller markets like Nashville and Michigan that are, you know, we're making investments in and we have higher growth. Yeah, I mean, it's like any portfolio of businesses where your high growth markets are gonna contribute more to, you know, unique customer acquisition.
Your mature markets, you're growing more through category expansion and growing more relevance with your customers through item penetration, selling more items, as well as, you know, growing in the outlying markets, you know, call it the higher income suburbs around the major cities, and that's how you grow in your mature markets. You know, we have 54 locations in 32 or 33 operating markets now. There's always a good balance between your more mature markets and then your high growth markets. I think, you know, we expect that the big investments that we've made in capacity, in infrastructure and sales force that we talked about are gonna drive, you know, a lot of our growth going forward.
Ben Wood
Vice President of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Okay. That's helpful. Just a follow-up on maybe some of the new restaurant openings you're seeing for your core end customers. Do you guys have an estimate on the pace that you're currently seeing in new restaurant openings, and how does that compare to maybe the current levels? It sounds like Chris has mentioned that it was faster than normal, potentially, but just wanted to make sure I understood that correctly.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Yeah. I think, you know, our numbers, you know, we're growing in new markets. You know, for us, it's new accounts, right? I don't think our systems differentiate between a new customer and a new opening. I think the numbers are a little fuzzy there. You know, I think Jim said before, you know, we had a 10% increase in customer base, overall. You know, part of that are brand new openings, and part of those are a lot of new customers for Chef. You know, what I could tell you anecdotally we've seen is a lot of development.
You know, when I look at Florida, you know, we see tremendous development in new neighborhoods, new buildings, and they're all adding restaurants. You know, restaurants, I think are, you know, how developers use as a reason for someone to come look at their building. I just continue to see, especially in the American market, you know, Dubai, we have tremendous amounts of openings constantly. In the US market, you know, you kinda see still a shifting of where people are choosing to live. You know, I still don't think we're at the what anyone would call normal, right? I don't know what normal is anymore. People are working hybrid.

I think restaurateurs and developers are kind of following, you know, following where people are migrating to, you know, to live, and they're building restaurants, and they're building apartments, and they're building homes. Ben Wood
Vice President of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Great. Thank you very much.
Chris Pappas
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, The Chefs' Warehouse
Thanks, Ben.

Chris Pappas

Andy.
Andrew Wolf
Senior Research Analyst, CL King & Associates

Andrew Wolf
Senior Research Analyst, CL King & Associates
